13        Before the Court is Timothy Himstreet and Montini Family Trust’s (collectively, 
14   “Proposed Intervenors” or “State Plaintiffs”) motion to intervene and stay or dismiss.  ECF No. 
15   127.  The Court will grant the motion and stay the case.              
16   I.   BACKGROUND                                                       
17        This derivative shareholder action arises out of defendant Wells Fargo’s alleged “breaches 
18   of fiduciary duty in connection with their failure to comply with federal law, including explicit 
19   regulatory requirements established by federal regulators in multiple consent orders since 2018[.]”  
20   ECF No. 116 at 4.                                                     
21        On January 2, 2024, City of Hollywood Firefighters’ Pension System (“City of 
22   Hollywood”) was selected as Lead Plaintiff in this action, ECF No. 105, and it filed its 
23   consolidated shareholder derivative complaint on February 16, 2024.  ECF No. 116.  The 
24   consolidated complaint asserts one claim of relief against the Individual Defendants for breach of 
25   fiduciary duty.1                                                      
26                                                                         

27                                                                         
    1 The Individual Defendants in the City of Hollywood action include Steven D. Black, Mark A. 
1        The earlier-filed action is Timothy Himstreet and Montini Family Trust v. Charles W. 
2   Scharf, et al., No. CGC-22-599223 (Cal. Super. Ct. April 19, 2022) (the “State Action”), a 
3   shareholder derivative action brought by Proposed Intervenors against Wells Fargo and its board 
4   of directors and officers, currently pending in San Francisco Superior Court.  It pleads claims for 
5   breach of fiduciary duty, unjust enrichment, and waste of corporate assets.  ECF No. 59-1 at 58–
6   60.  On October 5, 2022, the State Court issued an order overruling Wells Fargo’s demurrer to the 
7   complaint, id. at 68, which was thereafter affirmed by the Court of Appeal of the State of 
8   California, First Appellate District, id. at 81.                      
9        Proposed Intervenors now bring this motion to intervene pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 24, 
10   and to stay or dismiss pursuant to Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. United States, 424 
11   U.S. 800 (1976) (“Colorado River”).                                   
12   II.  DISCUSSION                                                       
13        A.   Mandatory Intervention                                      
14        Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24(a)(2) provides for intervention as a matter of right 
15   where the potential intervenor “claims an interest relating to the property or transaction that is the 
16   subject of the action, and is so situated that disposing of the action may as a practical matter 
17   impair or impede the movant’s ability to protect its interest, unless existing parties adequately 
18   represent that interest.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 24(a)(2).                  
19        An applicant for intervention as of right must satisfy four criteria:  “(1) the applicant must 
20   timely move to intervene; (2) the applicant must have a significantly protectable interest relating to 
21   the property or transaction that is the subject of the action; (3) the applicant must be situated such 
22   that the disposition of the action may impair or impede the party’s ability to protect that interest; 
23   and (4) the applicant’s interest must not be adequately represented by existing parties.”  Arakaki v. 
24   Cayetano, 324 F.3d 1078, 1083 (9th Cir. 2003) (citing Donnelly v. Glickman, 159 F.3d 405, 409 
25   (9th Cir. 1998)).  “Failure to satisfy any one of the requirements is fatal to the application, and [the 
26   Court] need not reach the remaining elements if one of the elements is not satisfied.”  Perry v. 
27   Proposition 8 Off. Proponents, 587 F.3d 947, 950 (9th Cir. 2009).     
1             1.   Significantly Protectable Interest                     
2        “The requirement of a significantly protectable interest is generally satisfied when ‘the 
3   interest is protectable under some law, and that there is a relationship between the legally 
4   protected interest and the claims at issue.’”  Araki, 324 F.3d at 1084 (quoting Sierra Club v. EPA, 
5   995 F.2d 1478, 1484 (9th Cir. 1993)).                                 
6        Proposed Intervenors recognize that, “unlike in a typical motion to intervene,” they “are 
7   not third parties seeking to participate in the Federal Action.”  ECF No. 127 at 15.  Rather, they 
8   contend that “[a]s a result of satisfying . . . demand futility requirements, [they] are now 
9   authorized to act on Wells Fargo’s behalf and to pursue the Company’s claims.”  Id.  City of 
10   Hollywood responds that “[t]he State Court’s order holding that demand was excused did nothing 
11   more than establish State Plaintiffs’ ‘standing to sue’ derivatively on behalf of Wells Fargo for the 
12   specific claims as to which demand was excused.”  ECF No. 134 at 12 (citing Advanced Advisors 
13   G. P. v. Berman, No. LACV1401420JAKSSX, 2014 WL 12772264, at *6 (C.D. Cal. Sept. 16, 
14   2014)).                                                               
15        “When conducting a demand futility analysis, a Delaware court proceeds on a claim-by-
16   claim and director-by-director basis.”  Ontario Provincial Council of Carpenters’ Pension Tr. 
17   Fund v. Walton, No. 2021-0827-JTL, 2023 WL 3093500, at *29 (Del. Ch. Apr. 26, 2023); see 
18   Beam v. Stewart, 833 A.2d 961, 977 n.48 (Del. Ch. 2003) (“Demand futility analysis is conducted 
19   on a claim-by-claim basis”), aff’d, 845 A.2d 1040 (Del. 2004).  If demand is excused as futile, it is 
20   solely “for the purposes of that claim.”  Ontario Provincial Council of Carpenters’ Pension Tr. 
21   Fund, 2023 WL 3093500, at *29.  Thus, “[i]f another set of claims arises out of a different nucleus 
22   of operative facts or concerns a different transaction, then the court moves on to the next claim and 
23   repeats the process.”  Id.                                            
24        Although Proposed Intervenors have standing to sue derivatively on behalf of Wells Fargo 
25   for specific claims, they cite no authority (and the Court is aware of none) that grants them a 
26   significantly protectable interest in order to seek a stay or dismissal of the federal action on “their 
27   behalf, in connection with their entitlement to pursue litigation for Wells Fargo[.]”  ECF No. 137 
1        “Failure to satisfy any one of the requirements is fatal” to a Rule 24(a) request.  Perry, 587 
2   F.3d at 950.  Because Proposed Intervenors have not demonstrated a significant protectable 
3   interest, their motion to intervene as of right is denied.  The Court declines to reach the remaining 
4   factors.                                                              
5        B.   Permissive Intervention                                     
6        Turning to permissive intervention, “[d]istrict courts have discretion to permit an entity to 
7   intervene if the entity raises a claim that has a legal or factual issue or issues in common with the 
8   underlying action.  In exercising their discretion, courts must consider whether intervention will 
9   unduly delay or prejudice the existing parties.”  In re Benny, 791 F.2d 712, 722 (9th Cir. 1986) 
10   (citing Fed. R. Civ. P. 24(b)(1)(B)) (“On timely motion, the court may permit anyone to intervene 
11   who . . . has a claim or defense that shares with the main action a common question of law or 
12   fact.”).                                                              
13        City of Hollywood concedes that Proposed Intervenors’ claims “share common questions 
14   of law and fact with [their] claims.”  ECF No. 134 at 13.  Therefore, permissive intervention in 
15   this case turns on whether intervention will unduly delay or prejudice the existing parties.  
16   Proposed Intervenors contend that their motion “is brought at an early stage in the federal 
17   proceedings and without any undue delay.”  ECF No. 127 at 20.  The Court agrees that the federal 
18   action is still in early stages—notably, the Court has yet to decide the question of demand futility.  
19   As a result, Proposed Intervenors have demonstrated that they are entitled to permissively 
20   intervene in this action.                                             
21        C.   Colorado River Stay or Dismissal                            
22        Having concluded that Proposed Intervenors are entitled to permissively intervene, the 
23   Court now addresses Proposed Intervenors’ Colorado River motion.      
24        “Generally, as between state and federal courts, the rule is that ‘the pendency of an action 
25   in the state court is no bar to proceedings concerning the same matter in the Federal court having 
26   jurisdiction.’”  Colorado River, 424 U.S. at 817 (quoting McClellan v. Carland, 217 U.S. 268, 282 
27   (1910)).  In rare cases, “there are principles unrelated to considerations of proper constitutional 
1   contemporaneous exercise of concurrent jurisdictions, either by federal courts or by state and 
2   federal courts.”  Colorado River, 424 U.S. at 817.  In the interest of “[w]ise judicial 
3   administration, giving regard to conservation of judicial resources and comprehensive disposition 
4   of litigation,” a district court can dismiss or stay a federal suit “due to the presence of a concurrent 
5   state proceeding”  Id. at 817–18.                                     
6        “No matter how the Colorado River doctrine is formally characterized, however, one 
7   principle is clear:  a stay of federal litigation in favor of state court proceedings ‘is the exception, 
8   not the rule.’”  Ernest Bock, LLC v. Steelman, 76 F.4th 827, 835 (9th Cir. 2023), cert. denied, 144 
9   S. Ct. 554 (2024) (quoting Colorado River, 424 U.S. at 813).  “Only the clearest of justifications 
10   will warrant” dismissal or a stay.  Colorado River, 424 U.S. at 813.      
11        The Ninth Circuit has articulated eight factors to determine whether a Colorado River stay 
12   is justified:  “(1) which court first assumed jurisdiction over any property at stake; (2) the 
13   inconvenience of the federal forum; (3) the desire to avoid piecemeal litigation; (4) the order in 
14   which the forums obtained jurisdiction; (5) whether federal law or state law provides the rule of 
15   decision on the merits; (6) whether the state court proceedings can adequately protect the rights of 
16   the federal litigants; (7) the desire to avoid forum shopping; and (8) whether the state court 
17   proceedings will resolve all issues before the federal court.”  R.R. St. & Co. Inc. v. Transp. Ins. 
18   Co., 656 F.3d 966, 978–79 (9th Cir. 2011).  The factors need not be evaluated like a “mechanical 
19   checklist,” but rather should be applied “in a pragmatic, flexible manner with a view to the 
20   realities of the case at hand.”  Moses H. Cone Mem’l Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 460 U.S. 1, 
21   21 (1983).  “The weight to be given to any one factor may vary greatly from case to case.”  Id. at 
22   16.2                                                                  
23             1.   Resolution of All Issues in State Court Proceedings    
24        Because “[p]arallelism is necessary but not sufficient to counsel in favor of abstention,” the 
25   Court addresses the final factor first.  Seneca Ins. Co., Inc. v. Strange Land, Inc., 862 F.3d 835,

24   in each of the cases do not overpower the overlapping facts and issues involved.”11  GreenPower

9             2.   Piecemeal Litigation                                   
10        “Piecemeal litigation occurs when different tribunals consider the same issue, thereby 
11   duplicating efforts and possibly reaching different results.”  Montanore Mins. Corp. v. Bakie, 867 
12   F.3d 1160, 1167 (9th Cir. 2017), as amended on denial of reh’g and reh’g en banc (Oct. 18, 2017) 
13   (quoting Am. Int’l Underwriters (Philippines), Inc. v. Cont’l Ins. Co., 843 F.2d 1253, 1258 (9th 
14   Cir. 1988)).  For this factor to favor a stay, “the case must raise a special concern about piecemeal 
15   litigation, which can be remedied by staying or dismissing the federal proceeding,” and which “the 
16   court could not have avoided by other means.”  Montanore Mins. Corp., 867 F.3d at 1167 (quoting 
17   R.R. St., 656 F.3d at 979) (internal quotation marks and alteration omitted). 
18        Proposed Intervenors argue that “[a]llowing the Federal Action to proceed would create the 
19   type of piecemeal litigation Colorado River and its progeny seek to avoid[.]”  ECF No. 127 at 24.  
20   In response, City of Hollywood contends that the risk of piecemeal litigation is slight because their 
21   claims “are broader and seek damages that [Proposed Intervenors] do not seek.”  ECF No. 134 at 
22   17.                                                                   
23        While there may be some slight differences between the state and federal actions, an 
24   indefeasible fact remains:  the core issue in each case—namely, state law breach of fiduciary 
25   duty—is the same.  “Discovery in both cases would require taking the depositions of the same

10             3.   Order Jurisdiction Was Obtained                        
11        “The order in which the forums obtained jurisdiction is not evaluated mechanically, but 
12   rather based on ‘the realities of the case at hand’ ‘in a pragmatic flexible manner.’”  GreenPower 
13   Motor Co., Inc., 2022 WL 21737783 at *5 (quoting Montanore Mins. Corp, 867 F.3d at 1168).  
14   For example, the Court accounts for the relative progress of the action in each forum.  See Am. 
15   Int’l Underwriters, 843 F.2d at 1257.                                 
16        Here, it is undisputed that the state action was filed before the federal action.  ECF No. 134 
17   at 18.  Additionally, Proposed Intervenors have already prevailed on their demand futility 
18   allegations and discovery is underway.  See ECF No. 59-1 at 5–6, 68, 81.  Thus, this factor favors 
19   Proposed Intervenors.                                                 
20             4.   Rule of Decision                                       
21        “The fact that state law provides the rule of decision on the merits in a case may favor a 
22   stay, but ‘only when the state law questions are themselves complex and difficult issues better 
23   resolved by a state court; it is not enough that a state law case is complex because it involves 
24   numerous parties or claims.’”  Montanore Mins. Corp, 867 F.3d at 1168 (quoting Seneca Ins. Co., 
25   Inc., 862 F.3d at 844.                                                
26        The parties agree that Delaware law governs the state-law claims in both the federal and 
27   state court actions.  See ECF No. 127 at 25–26; ECF No. 134 at 19.  Proposed Intervenors believe 
1   for nearly two years, and the State Court has already issued rulings on Wells Fargo’s demurrer, the 
2   individual defendants’ motion to strike, and three individual demurrers for failure to state a claim.”  
3   ECF No. 127 at 26.  City of Hollywood, on the other hand, argues that this factor is neutral 
4   because “[t]his Court is equally, if not better, equipped to apply Delaware law as compared to the 
5   State Court.”  ECF No. 134 at 19 (citing Sundquist on Behalf of Allstate Corp. v. Wilson, No. 18 
6   CV 3598, 2018 WL 6327007, at *5 (N.D. Ill. Dec. 4, 2018)) (“There is no dispute that . . . the 
7   governing law is Delaware law.  Neither this [federal] court nor the Illinois state court have any 
8   presumptive expertise in applying Delaware law.  This factor is therefore neutral, which disfavors 
9   abstention.”).                                                        
10        The Court agrees with City of Hollywood that neither this Court nor the state court is 
11   better suited to rule on Delaware law.  This factor is therefore neutral.   
12             5.   Adequacy of State Court                                
13        “A district court may not stay or dismiss the federal proceeding if the state proceeding 
14   cannot adequately protect the rights of the federal litigants.”  R.R. St., 656 F.3d at 981.  “For 
15   example, if there is a possibility that the parties will not be able to raise their claims in the state 
16   proceeding, a stay or dismissal is inappropriate.”  Id. (citing Moses H. Cone, 460 U.S. at 26).   
17        City of Hollywood “does not doubt the State Court’s competence to adjudicate State 
18   Plaintiffs’ claims.”  ECF No. 134 at 20.  Neither does this Court.  This factor favors Proposed 
19   Intervenors.                                                          
20             6.   Forum Shopping                                         
21        A Colorado River stay or dismissal is warranted “when it was readily apparent that the 
22   federal plaintiff was engaged in forum shopping.”  R.R. St., 656 F.3d at 981.  “Forum shopping 
23   refers to ‘[t]he practice of choosing the most favorable jurisdiction or court in which a claim might 
24   be heard.’”  Id. (quoting Black’s Law Dictionary (9th ed. 2009)).     
25        Proposed Intervenors argue that a stay or dismissal is warranted “even where there is no 
26   affirmative evidence of forum shopping because ‘allowing a substantially similar federal action to 
27   proceed would likely encourage forum shopping.’”  ECF No. 127 at 27 (quoting Gintz v. Jack in 
1   Hollywood points out that “[t]he Federal Action was not brought by any plaintiff who had 
2   previously brought the same claims in state court,” which often signals “serious concerns about 
3   forum shopping.”  ECF No. 134 at 20; see Nakash, 882 F.2d at 1413 (holding that this factor 
4   weighs “strongly in favor of abstention,” where the state plaintiff became “dissatisfied with the 
5   state court” and sought a “new [federal] forum for their claims.”).   
6        Although the federal action was filed later and contains substantial overlap with the state 
7   action, there is no evidence in the record from which to conclude that City of Hollywood engaged 
8   in forum shopping.  Cf. Bushansky, 2012 WL 3276937, at *5 (finding that there were “sufficient 
9   concerns of forum shopping” where the federal action appeared “vexatious and reactive.”).  
10   Accordingly, this factor favors City of Hollywood.                    
11        In sum, four of the six factors—including arguably the most important factor, 
12   parallelism—favor Proposed Intervenors; one of the remaining factors is neutral; and the other 
13   favors City of Hollywood.  Therefore, the Court concludes that this case presents sufficiently 
14   “exceptional circumstances” to justify a stay or dismissal under Colorado River.  See Colorado 
15   River, 424 U.S. at 813.                                               
16        D.   Stay or Dismissal                                           
17        The Ninth Circuit has instructed that “district courts must stay, rather than dismiss, an 
18   action when they determine that they should defer to the state court proceedings under Colorado 
19   River.”  Coopers & Lybrand v. Sun–Diamond Growers of CA, 912 F.2d 1135, 1138 (9th Cir. 
20   1990).  “This is in order to ensure that the federal forum will remain open if for some unexpected 
21   reason the state forum does turn out to be inadequate.”  Bushansky, 2012 WL 3276937, at *7 
22   (internal quotations and alterations omitted).  Accordingly, the instant action is stayed rather than 
23   dismissed.                                                            
24                              CONCLUSION                                 
25        For the foregoing reasons, Proposed Intervenors’ motion to stay is granted.  This action 
26   will be stayed until the state action is resolved.  The pending motions to dismiss and motion for 
27   joinder, ECF Nos. 130, 131, are also terminated without prejudice to re-filing, if appropriate.  The  
    1    parties shall file a status report within 10 days of the resolution of the state action and shall

15   River, 424 U.S. at 813.                                               
16        D.   Stay or Dismissal                                           
17        The Ninth Circuit has instructed that “district courts must stay, rather than dismiss, an 
18   action when they determine that they should defer to the state court proceedings under Colorado 
19   River.”  Coopers & Lybrand v. Sun–Diamond Growers of CA,
912 F.2d 1135, 1138
 (9th Cir. 
20   1990).  “This is in order to ensure that the federal forum will remain open if for some unexpected 
21   reason the state forum does turn out to be inadequate.”  Bushansky,
2012 WL 3276937
, at *7 
22   (internal quotations and alterations omitted).  Accordingly, the instant action is stayed rather than 
23   dismissed.                                                            
24                              CONCLUSION                                 
25        For the foregoing reasons, Proposed Intervenors’ motion to stay is granted.  This action 
26   will be stayed until the state action is resolved.  The pending motions to dismiss and motion for 
27   joinder, ECF Nos. 130, 131, are also terminated without prejudice to re-filing, if appropriate.  The  
    1    parties shall file a status report within 10 days of the resolution of the state action and shall
